{{< include latex-macros/macros.qmd >}}

In a **randomized controlled trial** (RCT),
treatment is assigned by the investigator using a random mechanism,
[independent](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/independence.html#def-indpt) of any characteristics of the participants.
Randomization makes the treatment groups **[exchangeable](#def-exchangeability)**:
the distribution of [potential outcomes](#def-potential-outcomes) is the same
in treated and untreated groups.

As a result, in a perfectly randomized trial:

$$
\ba
\E{Y(1)}
&= \E{Y(1) \mid A = 1} && \text{(unconditional exchangeability: } Y(1) \perp\!\!\!\perp A \text{)}
\\&= \E{Y \mid A = 1} && \text{(consistency: } Y = Y(1) \text{ when } A = 1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

and similarly for the control group:

$$
\ba
\E{Y(0)}
&= \E{Y(0) \mid A = 0} && \text{(unconditional exchangeability: } Y(0) \perp\!\!\!\perp A \text{)}
\\&= \E{Y \mid A = 0} && \text{(consistency: } Y = Y(0) \text{ when } A = 0 \text{)}
\ea
$$

The observed mean difference between treatment groups
is an [unbiased](https://morrison-lab.github.io/sds/estimation.html#def-unbiased) estimate of the [ATE](#def-ate):

$$\widehat{\text{ATE}} = \bar{Y}_{A=1} - \bar{Y}_{A=0}$$

::: notes

Randomization achieves unconditional exchangeability:
$A \perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0), Y(1))$.
Because there are no common causes of treatment assignment
and the outcome,
there is no [confounding](#def-confounding-obs).
The observed association between $A$ and $Y$ in the data
is a direct measure of the causal effect.

:::

## The HERS study: a randomized trial example {#sec-causal-hers-rct}

<!-- Included file paths are relative to the project root (standard for Quarto) -->
{{< include _subfiles/shared/_sec_hers_intro.qmd >}}

In HERS, hormone therapy (HT) was randomized,
so the treatment groups were [exchangeable](#def-exchangeability) at baseline.
The observed difference in CHD event rates between
the HT and placebo groups estimates the causal effect of HT.

{{< include _subfiles/shared/_sec_hers_conclusions.qmd >}}

::: notes

The HERS result illustrates the gap between
observational evidence and causal evidence:
prior observational studies had suggested large benefits of HT,
but these reflected confounding by
the "healthy user" effect —
women who voluntarily used HT tended to be healthier overall.
Randomization in HERS removed this confounding.

:::

## Covariate adjustment in RCTs {#sec-causal-rct-adjustment}

Although randomization ensures no [confounding](#def-confounding-obs),
adjusting for baseline [covariates](Intro-to-GLMs.qmd#def-predictors) in an RCT can still be useful:

- **Improved [precision](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/variance-covariance.html#def-precision)**: Adjusting for strong predictors of the outcome
  reduces residual variance and narrows [confidence intervals](https://morrison-lab.github.io/sds/inference.html#def-confidence-interval).
- **Covariate imbalance**: When randomization produces chance imbalances
  in small trials,
  adjustment can correct for these baseline differences.

However, in an RCT,
covariates that are **[mediators](#def-mediator)** of the treatment effect
(i.e., variables affected by treatment)
should generally **not** be adjusted for
when estimating the **total** causal effect of treatment.
Adjusting for mediators blocks part of the causal pathway
and gives only the **direct** effect of treatment.
